thermoblock.paragraph: A single shared thermoblock or thermocoil heats water in a small flow path rather than using separate brew and steam boilers. Animate the shot first, then a switch to the hotter steam mode, a model-specific wait for the ready indication and a condensation purge, then milk steaming. Before another shot, show the machine returning to brewing conditions using its prescribed cooldown or purge; on Breville’s Thermocoil Barista Express this purge happens automatically into the drip tray. Do not draw brew and steam flowing simultaneously through one shared heating path. Classic thermostat-boiler temperature surfing is not a generic required step here: use the model’s controller and readiness procedure. Separate brew and steam thermoblocks are a different architecture and may permit simultaneous operation when the maker explicitly says so.
steps: Reach model-specific brew-ready state; prepare and extract espresso.
Stop extraction; select steam mode.
Wait for the steam-ready signal and purge condensation as the manual directs.
Texture milk; stop steam, then clean and purge the wand.
Return to brewing mode and complete the model-specific temperature reset, automatically on some designs, before the next extraction.
notes: The sequence is a shared-heater schematic, not a universal control-button procedure.
No numerical steam-switch wait is assigned. The BES870 manual uses a flashing-to-steady light.
ThermoJet and Thermocoil are preserved as maker terms in individual machine records; they are not evidence of identical construction.
The single-path limitation must not be applied to dual-heater machines.

singleBoiler.paragraph: One brew-and-steam boiler must work at two different temperatures, so the operations are sequential. Animate brew-ready water feeding the shot, stop brewing, select steam, purge condensation and wait for the steam-ready indication, then steam the milk. After steaming, turn steam mode off and follow the maker’s refill/cooldown procedure before returning to brew-ready state. For example, Silvia’s manual ends by operating the hot-water switch and wand until water comes out, then closing both controls. On a thermostat-controlled machine, temperature surfing means timing the next shot to a repeatable point in the heating cycle; it is separate from the steam-to-brew refill and has no universal wait. PID controls the setpoint rather than requiring that manual cycle-timing routine, but does not turn a shared boiler into simultaneous brew-and-steam hardware.
steps: Warm and reach the brew-ready state. If using a thermostat-surfing routine, establish its repeatable cycle landmark before the shot.
Brew, then stop extraction.
Select steam mode, purge condensation and wait for the maker’s ready indication.
Steam milk; stop delivery and steam mode.
Purge/clean wand and refill the boiler as the maker directs.
Return to brew temperature/readiness before another shot; do not animate immediate brewing at steam temperature.

sources.locator: pp.9–10; p.10 rendered to verify step order

sources.type: specialist retailer technical education; explainer only

notes: The Silvia manual’s exact order is switch steam off, purge, clean, then use the hot-water switch and open tap until water appears.
Heating-light behavior varies by machine. No generic light-on/light-off rule or seconds value is assigned.
Do not apply this steam sequence to espresso-only single-boiler machines without steam.

heatExchanger.paragraph: An HX machine keeps its main boiler hot enough to supply steam while fresh brew water travels through a separate heat-exchange circuit; the two water paths do not mix. Animate warm-up of the boiler and group first, then any model-required cooling flush before the shot, then brew water flowing to the coffee while steam can flow to the wand at the same time. There is no brew-to-steam temperature-mode change, so there is no switching wait of the single-boiler type. Traditional HX temperature management may use a cooling flush after idle, which is not the same procedure as timing a thermostat-controlled single boiler’s heating cycle. Follow the exact model’s manual: neither a fixed flush duration nor a universal need for flushing follows merely from the label HX or PID.
steps: Heat the main boiler and bring the group to its required operating state.
Apply a cooling flush only where the exact machine’s instructions call for it.
Start the shot through the separate fresh-water heat-exchange path.
Steam can run concurrently from the main boiler.
Stop brew and steam independently; no temperature-mode reset is inherently required between them.

sources.type: specialist retailer technical education; explainer only

notes: This is architecture-level behavior, not proof that a particular machine has an unrestricted simultaneous operating mode.
No generic warm-up, recovery or cooling-flush duration is assigned.
ECM’s 3C temperature-monitoring description is not treated as a generic HX feature.

dualBoiler.paragraph: A dual-boiler machine separates the brew-water boiler from the steam boiler, allowing each to operate at its own temperature. Animate both reaching their operating states, then extraction from the brew boiler and steam from the steam boiler either sequentially or concurrently. No shared boiler has to rise to steam temperature or cool back down between those operations, although initial heating and recovery still depend on the model and electrical controls. A PID-controlled brew boiler manages its setpoint without the manual thermostat-cycle timing called temperature surfing; this is not a promise of zero thermal drift. If the steam boiler is switched off, it must be enabled and heated before steaming. Simultaneous operation is a maker-verified capability on the Breville BES920, not an inference to apply automatically to every two-boiler product.
steps: Enable and warm the required boilers; use the maker’s brew/steam readiness indications.
Extract espresso from the brew boiler.
Steam from the separate steam boiler, concurrently if the model supports it.
Stop each output; retain their separate temperature states.
Before subsequent drinks, allow any model-specific recovery; no brew-to-steam mode change is inherently needed.

sources.type: specialist retailer technical education; explainer only

notes: No numerical recovery time is inferred from boiler count.
Dual boilers are not the only architecture able to brew and steam simultaneously.
PID is temperature regulation, not independent proof of measured temperature accuracy or absence of drift.
